title: The Investigative Question and Data Collection
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 1.10 The Investigative Question and Data Collection
intro: Identify study designs and variables, frame investigative questions, and distinguish population generalization from causal conclusions.

moments.title: Investigative questions
moments.text: Specify the population, variables, and purpose of the study.

moments.title: Estimate or test a claim
moments.text: A question determines the analysis needed.

moments.title: A census
moments.text: Collect information from every unit in the population.

moments.title: Random samples
moments.text: A random selection mechanism supports population generalization.

moments.title: Experiments
moments.text: Researchers impose treatments on experimental units.

moments.title: Fertilizer example
moments.text: Identify plots, fertilizer treatments, and measured growth.

moments.title: Prospective and retrospective
moments.text: Distinguish following units forward from examining past records.

moments.title: Confounding
moments.text: An associated third variable can provide an alternative explanation.

moments.title: Scope of conclusions
moments.text: Random selection and random assignment answer different questions.

cards.name: Census or sample?
cards.text: A census seeks data from every population member; a sample observes a subset.

cards.name: Experiment or observational study?
cards.text: An experiment imposes treatments. An observational study records existing conditions.

cards.name: Random selection
cards.text: Supports generalizing to the population from which the sample was drawn.

cards.name: Random assignment
cards.text: Supports a causal comparison of treatments in a well-designed experiment.

cards.name: Question components
cards.text: Specify variables, an estimation or testing goal, and the population or causal comparison.

questions.obj: Identify the components of an experiment
questions.q: The video proposes 30 equally sized grass plots, assigned fertilizer A, fertilizer B, or no fertilizer. The plots are watered and growth is recorded. Identify units, factor, treatments, and response.

work.text: Each grass plot is an experimental unit.

steps.t: Identify the factor and its levels.

work.text: The factor is fertilizer treatment. Its levels are A, B, and no fertilizer.
The response is grass growth, measured consistently after treatment.

questions.answer: There are three treatments. Watering all plots consistently controls a condition; it is not an extra treatment factor here.

traps.title: Random selection versus assignment
traps.weak: Random assignment makes the volunteers representative of everyone.
traps.better: Random assignment supports treatment comparison; random selection supports population generalization.

traps.title: Association versus cause
traps.weak: Students who sleep longer score higher, so sleep caused the difference.
traps.better: An observational association may have alternative explanations involving variables related to both sleep and scores.

traps.title: Confounding without a connection
traps.weak: Any other variable is a confounder.
traps.better: A plausible confounding variable must be associated with both the explanatory and response variables.

traps.title: A vague investigative question
traps.better: Does the treatment increase mean growth compared with no treatment for the specified population of plants?

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: A random sample uses a chance mechanism; equal individual selection probabilities alone do not define an SRS. Nonrandom samples still provide descriptive information, but population generalization requires caution.

questions.stem: A researcher asks adults about existing exercise habits and records current blood pressure without assigning exercise. The study is:
why: The description does not include all adults in a defined population.

questions.stem: Researchers recruit volunteers, then randomly assign two revision methods. What does random assignment primarily support?
opts: A causal comparison of the methods
why: Random assignment helps separate treatment effects from pre-existing differences.
Volunteers are not a random sample of every student.
A census observes the whole population.

questions.stem: A study selects people today and examines their medical records from the past five years. It is:
why: A prospective study follows units into the future.
Past records are examined after selecting units now.
The size and scope do not imply a census.

questions.stem: A study compares screen time and headaches. Which explanation describes a plausible confounder?
opts: Workload, if it is related to both screen time and headaches
why: An arbitrary ID is not an alternative explanation.
Sample size is not a third variable on the people.
Workload could account for part of the observed association.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A university wants to know whether a new reminder system increases the proportion of students returning library books on time. It randomly samples students from its current enrollment list and randomly assigns sampled students to receive reminders or usual service.
parts: (a) State an investigative question with population, response, and direction.
(b) Identify the units, explanatory variable, treatments, and response variable.
(c) Explain the roles of the two random processes.
sample: (a) For currently enrolled university students, does the new reminder system increase the proportion of library returns made on time compared with usual service?

(b) Students are the experimental units. The explanatory variable is reminder condition, with treatments new reminders and usual service. The response records whether each student's specified return is on time; the measurement plan should specify one comparable return per student.

(c) Random selection supports generalizing to currently enrolled university students. Random assignment supports a causal comparison of reminders with usual service, assuming the experiment is implemented appropriately.
checklist: Specifies an increase and a measurable response.
Names both treatments and the response.
